title: Rust FFI tokenizer + cooperative threadpool: empirical notes and tuning
content:
Summary:

This note summarises a set of exploratory experiments focused on CPU-side serving bottlenecks caused by tokenization and request pre-processing in the Python runtime. The goal was to compare: (A) pure-Python tokenization on request thread, (B) offloading tokenization to a Rust FFI (pyo3) worker, and (C) a hybrid cooperative threadpool model where small requests are handled inline and larger jobs are offloaded. We also measured the interaction with the request parsing layer (JSON deserialization) and threadpool sizing/affinity.

Why this matters:
- At low token counts, Python call overhead and GIL contention dominate tail latency.
- At high qps, naive background workers can cause context switching and increase p95/p99.
- We need concrete tuning guidance for default container images and dedicated capacity profiles.

Environment and methodology:
- Runtime image: rwinf/serve-2025-01 (CPython 3.11.4, pypy not tested here)
- Tokenizer versions: python-tokenize-v1 (baseline, pure Python loop using regex + byte-level ops) vs rust-tokenize-v0.9 (pyo3 binding exposing tokenize(text) -> tokens)
- JSON libraries: std json (json.loads), ujson 5.8.0, orjson 3.11.0 tested for parse perf
- Hardware: c6i.8xlarge equivalent (32 vCPU), pinned 8 vCPU container for experiments to simulate small dedicated worker slot; tests repeated on 16 vCPU and 4 vCPU configs for scaling curves
- Workloads: synthetic HTTP requests with varied payloads: short prompt (30 tokens average, 120 bytes), medium (150 tokens, 600 bytes), long (800 tokens, 3.2 KB). Concurrency sweep from 1 to 200 concurrent connections using vegeta-style load generator.
- Metrics: latency p50/p95/p99 (end-to-end), CPU user/sys %, context-switches/s, per-thread busy time (via perf), GIL hold times (pyinstrument + custom tracer), and syscall breakdown.
- Profiling tools: Linux perf, py-spy flamegraphs, eBPF (bcc) traces for schedule latency, strace sampling for syscall distribution.

Key experiments and results (abridged):

1) Baseline: pure-Python tokenize on request thread
- Observations: for short prompts, median latency 18ms, p95 52ms, p99 120ms at 50 qps. CPU per-request dominated by Python bytecode overhead and GIL acquisition: GIL hold time averaged 3.5ms per request for small prompts. Context-switch rate low but many short-lived Python frames.
- For medium prompts, p50 45ms, p95 120ms. For long prompts, bulk tokenization cost grows linearly as expected; p99 dominated by tokenization plus GC pauses (minor).
- Bottleneck: pure-Python tokenizer cost + GIL contention during high concurrency.

2) Rust FFI offload (synchronous call into pyo3 bound tokenizer)
- Implementation: single synchronous call tokenize(text) that returns token ids as Python list of ints. The pyo3 wrapper releases the GIL during heavy Rust work where possible and returns a list.
- Short prompts: median latency 12ms, p95 30ms, p99 80ms at 50 qps. Improvement primarily due to lower CPU cycles spent in Python loops and decreased GIL hold — the pyo3 call performs work outside the GIL for most of the heavy lifting.
- However, at high concurrency (>120 concurrent requests) we observed increased syscalls and kernel scheduling overhead: the Rust code spawns internal threads to parallelize rare long tokenization calls which interacted poorly with our container's cgroup CPU quota, producing higher p99 than expected.
- Memory note: returning Python lists of ints for long sequences had measurable overhead (time to materialize list and refcounting on return).

3) Cooperative threadpool model (hybrid):
- Design: small requests (<=64 tokens) tokenized inline in the request worker (fast path). Larger requests are posted to a bounded threadpool implemented in Rust and polled back via a completion queue; we avoid constructing large Python lists by returning a bytes-packed token buffer and mapping into Python with a memoryview that parses in-place.
- Results: across the board this gave the best tail-latency for mixed workloads. For 1:1 traffic mix of short/medium/long at 150 concurrent connections: p50 15ms, p95 45ms, p99 90ms. Under heavy long-request fraction (>60% long) background pool saturation increased queueing but still kept short-request latencies stable because of the fast path.
- Overheads: complexity increased (completion queue bookkeeping, careful memory ownership). We measured lower GIL hold times for medium/long requests because most heavy work stays outside CPython.

4) JSON parsing microbench: orjson vs ujson vs std
- For request pre-processing, switching from json.loads to orjson.loads reduced CPU per-request for medium payloads by ~30% and improved p95 by ~12% under mid concurrency. ujson was slightly faster than std but had correctness issues for some edge-case iso8601 timestamps. Recommendation: orjson as default in the image.

5) Threadpool sizing and CPU affinity experiments
- Naive: unbounded worker pool or pool sized to available vCPUs led to increased context switches and p99 spikes when mixed short+long workloads present.
- Heuristic we tested: pool_size = max(2, min(available_cpus // 4, 16)) for the Rust background pool + fast-path inline tokenization threshold. This reduced context switches and kept background worker queue latency acceptable.
- CPU pinning: pinning worker threads to a subset of cores (separate core set for request pollers vs heavy tokenizers) reduced interference and improved p99 by ~18% in 16 vCPU tests. Linux isolcpus + sched_setaffinity used in experiments.

Profiling artifacts (high level):
- Flamegraphs show reduction in Python-layer stacks when using Rust offload: baseline had long chains in tokenizer.py:tokenize -> regex.finditer -> PyObject_Call; rust offload removed most of that.
- perf top showed high syscalls for futex/wake at high concurrency in the pure-Rust-threaded variant — indicates contention on mutex-based queues. We rewrote a hot queue path to use lock-free ring buffer for improved latency.

Concrete numbers (representative):
- Workload: mixed 50/30/20 short/medium/long, 150 concurrent
  - Baseline pure-Python: p50 22ms, p95 68ms, p99 180ms, CPU % ~78
  - Rust FFI synchronous: p50 14ms, p95 36ms, p99 105ms, CPU % ~82 (more kernel activity)
  - Hybrid cooperative: p50 15ms, p95 44ms, p99 92ms, CPU % ~75 (lower variability)

Actionable recommendations:
1) Adopt orjson as default parser in request preproc image. It gives immediate win with very low risk.
2) Provide a Rust-based tokenizer FFI in the base image that releases the GIL and returns a compact buffer representation (not Python list) for long outputs.
3) Implement hybrid fast-path: default threshold 64 tokens for inline tokenize; larger requests offloaded to bounded background pool with capacity = max(2, min(cpus//4, 16)). Tunable via REDWOOD_TOKENIZER_POOL env var.
4) Expose CPU pinning knobs in Dedicated container profiles (document config and recommended defaults). For Dedicated 8vCPU worker use: worker_affinity_cores=0-3, tokenizer_affinity_cores=4-7.
5) Avoid creating Python lists for tokens for >256 tokens; instead return a bytes buffer or memoryview and parse lazily in Python only as-needed.
6) Add monitoring: instrument GIL hold time histogram, background pool queue length, ring-buffer contention metric, and per-request syscalls count. Surface p99 regression alerts tied to these metrics.

Open questions / next steps:
- Validate on real traffic for dedicated capacity profiles (customer beta). Synthetic mixes are good but not identical to user distributions.
- Evaluate PyPy and subinterpreters for avoiding GIL contention in small-request dominated workloads. Early tests with subinterpreters showed reduced GIL hold times but complexity in C-extension lifecycle.
- Consider a tokenization cache for frequent prefixes (KV cache interplay) — this could dramatically reduce CPU for chat-like workloads.
- Re-evaluate memory ownership APIs: avoid copying between Rust/Python for token buffers where possible.

Appendix: quick TODOs and links
- PR: github PR above implements initial pyo3 binding and ring-buffer queue. Needs review for memory safety and GC edge-cases.
- JIRA SRV-7321 tracks integrating orjson and runtime flags.
- Slack thread for experiments: link above.

Notes to reviewers: this doc is a working experiment summary. Code and microbench scripts are in the PR; please run the suite if you have capacity. Questions about GC vs tokenization interaction are noted in the PR comments.

End of note.
